nameStory: The name 'clammy' comes from the plant's sticky, glandular stem that feels damp and tacky to the touch - like clammy skin on a humid day. 'Hedge-hyssop' refers to its traditional use as a medicinal herb similar to true hyssop, though it's not actually related to that Mediterranean plant.
description: Clammy hedge-hyssop is a small, unassuming annual wildflower that you might easily walk past without noticing. This modest plant grows up to about a foot tall with a sticky stem and pairs of oval leaves arranged opposite each other up the stem. Its tiny white tubular flowers bloom in small clusters, each flower only about half an inch long with five pointed sepals at the base that look like little green fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small annual herb reaching only about 12 inches tall with a distinctly sticky, glandular stem that feels tacky when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped to oval leaves up to 2 inches long, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, sometimes with small teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny whitish tubular flowers about half an inch long, nearly cylindrical in shape, arranged in loose clusters along the upper stem

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules about a quarter-inch wide that split open to release tiny seeds

idTips.label: Stem Texture
idTips.description: Stem feels noticeably sticky and clammy due to tiny glands that produce a tacky secretion - this is the plant's signature feature

habitat: Look for clammy hedge-hyssop in wet meadows, pond edges, stream banks, and other consistently moist to wet areas throughout New England. It thrives in muddy or sandy soils that stay damp, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll typically find it in open or partially shaded spots rather than deep forest.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes in late spring, with the characteristic sticky stems becoming apparent as they begin to grow taller.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with tiny white flowers appearing in loose clusters. The sticky, glandular stem is most noticeable during warm, humid summer weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small round seed capsules develop and split open. Plants begin to decline as this annual completes its life cycle.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain as this is an annual plant. Seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Despite being called 'neglecta' (meaning 'overlooked'), this little plant was actually used by Native Americans and early settlers as a powerful medicinal herb - but it's quite toxic and was sometimes called 'poor man's digitalis' because it affects the heart similarly to the dangerous foxglove plant.
confusionNotes: The sticky stem is your best clue to separate this from other small wetland plants with white flowers. If it doesn't feel clammy and tacky when you gently touch the stem, it's probably something else entirely.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'neglecta' literally means 'neglected' or 'overlooked,' which perfectly describes how most people walk right past this inconspicuous little plant. Despite its humble appearance, it belongs to the same family as snapdragons and was once considered part of the figwort family before botanical classification changes.
compareHints: Clammy hedge-hyssop differs from its relative golden hedge-hyssop mainly in flower color - golden hedge-hyssop has bright yellow flowers instead of white ones. Both share the characteristic sticky, glandular stems, but golden hedge-hyssop is much less common in New England. The white flowers and more widespread distribution help distinguish the clammy species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Golden hedge-hyssop differs from its close relative clammy hedge-hyssop primarily by flower color - golden has bright yellow blooms while clammy has small white or pale yellow flowers.
